The analogy is DNA as a map and clue. Sometimes the map answers "who is close to whom?". This is the question of the matrix `G`. Sometimes the map shows a region marked with strong signal. This is the question of GWAS. Sometimes we use the whole map to estimate the probable path of a young animal before having many offspring evaluated. This is the question of genomic prediction.

Matrix `G` is a map of molecular kinship. Two animals may have similar pedigree, but share more or less markers than expected. The matrix `G` tries to summarize this similarity observed in the markers.

GWAS is a local track search. It looks SNP for SNP and asks if any marker is associated with phenotypic difference. The result is usually seen as Manhattan plot: each point is a marker, and high peaks indicate stronger statistical association. Pico is not automatic proof of causal gene; it is a point that deserves investigation.

Genomic prediction is the use of all markers to predict. Instead of focusing on a peak, it uses many small signals at the same time. GBLUP is a form of prediction that uses genomic kinship, in matrix `G`, within the logic of mixed models. The practical question is: does prediction work in animals that were not used to train the model?

The analogy is to adjust a cake ruler before measuring the animals. If a ruler starts 2 cm above zero, every measure taken with it is greater. It is not worth saying that an animal measured with this ruler is larger without correcting the error of the ruler. First we correct the ruler; then we compare the animals.

Farm can function as a cake ruler. Sex can also work like this. If males are heavier on average than females, compare a male from a good farm with a female from a bad animal mixture farm, sex and environment. The model tries to answer: how much of the measure belongs to the known group and how much remains for the animal and for the error?

Fixed effect is like a ruler that we want to adjust directly. If the course compares exactly two farms and two sexes, we can estimate the average difference between these groups and correct the measure. Random effect is different: it represents levels seen as a sample of a larger population of effects. Residue is what remains after the model explained what was foreseen in the formula.

before:
The analogy is a genetic bar code. A product bar code does not describe the entire product, but helps to identify patterns. A SNP panel works similarly. It does not read the entire genome in full detail; it observes many specific points where animals may differ.

A SNP is a variation in a DNA position. In one position, some animals may have the `A` allele and others may have `B` the allele. As horses are diploids, each animal carries two copies of that point, one inherited from the father and one from the mother. Therefore, if we are counting the `B` allele, the genotype can be coded as `0`, `1` or `2`.

The code `0` means no copy of the allele counted. The code `1` means a copy. The code `2` means two copies. The biology behind it is simple: `0` can represent `AA`, `1` can account for `AB`, and `2` may represent `BB`, when `B` is the allele we are counting. The exact letter depends on the marker; the logic of counting is the same.

before:
The central formula of the unit is:

`DEP = EBV / 2`

Where:

- `DEP` is the expected difference in progeny;
- `EBV` is the estimated genetic value of the animal;
- both must be in the same unit of the characteristic;
- dividing by 2 represents the average expectation of transmission to offspring.

If a stallion has `EBV = 20` points for a didactic performance index, then:

`DEP = 20 / 2 = 10`

Biologically, this means that, on average, the progeny of this stallion is expected to have 10 more points than the basis of comparison, in the conditions and assumptions of the evaluation. It does not mean that all offspring will be 10 upper points. DEP is average expectation, not individual promise.

We will also use a simple phenotypic correction:

`fenotipo_corrigido = fenotipo_observado - efeito_ambiente`

Here, `efeito_ambiente` is a didactic adjustment of a known effect. If an animal had an environment advantage of `+8` points, we removed this advantage to compare more fairly. This is not yet a linear model, mixed model or BLUP. In M16, this type of adjustment will be formalized with models; in M17, it will be linked to genetic evaluation with BLUP.

before:
The central formula is:

`R = h2 * S`

Where:

- `R` is the expected response to selection, in the unit of the characteristic per generation;
- `h2` is the heritability in the restricted sense, without unity, between 0 and 1 in the exercise;
- `S` is the selection differential, in the unit of the characteristic.

If `h2 = 0,30` and `S = 20` points, then:

`R = 0,30 * 20 = 6`

Biologically, the next generation is expected 6 points above the original average, not 20 points. The 20 points represent the average phenotypic superiority of the selected parents. The expected response is lower because only part of this superiority is attributed to additive genetic variation.

To consider time, we used:

`ganho_por_ano = R / L`

Where `L` is the generation interval in years. If `R = 6` points per generation and `L = 8` years:

`ganho_por_ano = 6 / 8 = 0,75`

This means that the expected average gain, distributed by time, is 0,75 point per year. Biological gain happens per generation, but planning needs to see time.

before:
The central formula is:

`VP = VA + VD + VI + VE`

Where:

- `VP` is the total phenotypic variance;
- `VA` is the additive genetic variance;
- `VD` is the dominance variance;
- `VI` is the variance of epistatic interaction;
- `VE` is the environmental variance.

All terms are on the same variance scale. If the example uses points of variance, all components are also points of variation. If the characteristic was measured in g/day, a real variance would be in `(g/dia)^2`.

This sum is a simple partition within the model adopted in the exercise. It assumes that the components are being treated separately and does not include other possible sources or relationships, such as covariances between components or genotype-environment interaction. Therefore, the formula is a class organization tool, not a universal law for any data design.

We will also use the additive fraction:

`h2 = VA / VP`

In this unit, `h2` will be used only as the fraction of the phenotypic variance explained by `VA`, because the task of M8 asks to interpret this fraction. The most complete interpretation of heritability is for M9. Here, the use is operational: calculate the additive fraction to understand why `VA` is central to selection.

If `VA = 40` and `VP = 100`, then:

`h2 = 40 / 100 = 0,40`

Biologically, this means that 40% of the phenotypic variation of the example is in the additive part of the model. It does not mean that 40% of the phenotype of an individual animal is "genetic". The account speaks of the variation between animals of a population, not of the composition of an isolated animal.

before:
The didactic formula of the manual calculation of this unit is:

`EBV_didatico = h2 * y`

Where:

- `y` is the phenotypic deviation of the animal in relation to the average of the comparable group;
- `h2` is the heritability in the restricted sense, in scale from `0` to `1`;
- `EBV_didatico` is a simple shrinked prediction in the same unit of `y`.

If the young stallion had `y = 20` points and the characteristic has `h2 = 0,30`, then:

`EBV_didatico = 0,30 * 20 = 6`

Biologically, the number `6` says: the gross difference of `20` points should not be read as `20` points of additive genetic merit. With moderate heritability, part of the observed difference can come from environment and residue. The value collected is lower because the model does not transfer all the observation to the genetic value.

This calculation is not BLUP complete. The name `EBV_didatico` is only a pedagogical label for a simple shrink prediction. The complete BLUP adjusts fixed effects, uses kinship relationships, combines information from several animals and depends on variance components. The miniature serves for the student to see the principle before entering the matrix.

The factor `lambda` helps to understand the shrinkage force. In the simplified case of this class, assuming that the phenotypic variation was separated into additive genetic and residual part, we can write:

`lambda = (1 - h2) / h2`

If `h2 = 0,30`, then:

`lambda = 0,70 / 0,30 = 2,33`

Higher value of `lambda` indicates that the residue weighs more than the additive genetic variation. In this case, the model should rely less on raw individual deviation and shrink more prediction. If `h2` increases, `lambda` decreases, and the observed deviation receives more genetic weight.

before:
The general correlation formula is:

`r = covxy / sqrt(vx * vy)`

Where:

- `r` is the correlation between the characteristics `x` and `y`;
- `covxy` is the covariance between `x` and `y`;
- `vx` is the variance of `x`;
- `vy` is the variance of `y`;
- `sqrt(vx * vy)` standardizes covariance for scale from -1 to 1.

If `x` is weight and `y` is fat thickness, the formula measures how much the weight and fat deviations go together, adjusting for the size of the variation of each characteristic.

For different types of correlation, the logic is the same, but the components change:

`rP = covPxy / sqrt(VPx * VPy)`

`rA = covAxy / sqrt(VAx * VAy)`

`rE = covExy / sqrt(VEx * VEy)`

`rP` uses covariance and phenotypic variances. `rA` uses covariance and additive genetic variances. `rE` uses covariance and environmental variances. The error we want to avoid is to look `rP` and automatically conclude that the association is genetic.

before:
BLUP means `Best Linear Unbiased Prediction`, or better linear prediction not biased. In animal breeding, BLUP is used to predict random effects, especially additive genetic values. The term "best" depends on the assumptions of the model and the variances used. Therefore, BLUP is not an automatic biological truth. It is a statistical prediction conditioned to the model.

The animal model is a mixed model in which each animal receives its own additive genetic effect. The basic writing is:

`y = Xb + Za + e`

In this formula, `y` contains the observed phenotypes; `Xb` represents fixed effects, such as farm, sex or contemporary group; `Za` links each observation to the additive genetic value of the animal; and `e` is the residue. The vector `a` contains the additive genetic values to be predicted. When we talk about `EBV`, we are talking about the estimation of these additive genetic values.

The central difference in relation to M16 is that now the random effect `a` is not a collection of loose deviations. It has covariance given by the matrix `A`. In conceptual form:

`a ~ N(0, A * sigma_a^2)`

This means that the additive genetic values of the animals are related as expected. If two animals are more related, their expected additive genetic values have higher covariance. If they are less related, the expected covariance is lower. The matrix `A` is the numerical way of placing the pedigree within the model.

The mixed model equations, or `MME`, gather fixed effects and random effects in a single system. For conceptual reading, a simplified form is:

`[X'X  X'Z; Z'X  Z'Z + A^-1 * lambda] [b_hat; a_hat] = [X'y; Z'y]`

The student does not need to solve this matrix by hand in this unit. The formula serves to locate the pieces of the model, not to train matrix algebra. `X` adjusts fixed effects. `Z` binds observations to the animals. `A^-1` inserts kinship. `lambda` controls the relative weight between residue and additive genetic variation. When the residue weighs too much in relation to additive genetics, the model shrinks more `EBV` to the average.

Susceptibility is the latent tendency of an animal to express an unwanted outcome, such as disease. Greater susceptibility means a greater chance of crossing the manifestation threshold. For desired outcomes, such as pregnancy or survival, the same logic can be explained as latent propensity to success. This distinction avoids treating every result as if it were disease.

Prevalence is the proportion of animals that appears in the category of interest. If 18 of 100 horses have a disease, the observed prevalence of the disease is 18%. If 72 of 100 mares are pregnant, the prevalence of pregnancy is 72%. The prevalence is observable; the underlying scale is a didactic way to explain why the registration yes / cannot yet have a quantitative basis.

Griffiths et al. (2016) present examples of susceptibility traits to diseases and underlying traits studied by QTL. Threshold trait is a trait observed in categories, but interpreted as a result of a continuous underlying scale. The category appears when this scale exceeds a threshold. Instead of directly measuring the underlying scale, we observed the final result: affected or not affected, pregnant or empty, alive or dead.

Susceptibility is the latent tendency of an animal to express an unwanted outcome, such as disease. Greater susceptibility means a greater chance of crossing the manifestation threshold. For desired outcomes, such as pregnancy or survival, the same logic can be explained as latent propensity to success. This distinction avoids treating every result as if it were disease.

If 72 of 100 mares are pregnant, the prevalence of pregnancy is 72%. before:
Threshold characteristics require caution because the observed category hides distance to the threshold. Two unaffected horses may have very different underlying positions. Two lots with the same prevalence may have different underlying distributions. One lot can have many animals close to the threshold and another can have few.

Genetics can change yes/no response by contributing to the displacement of the underlying scale. If a group has higher average susceptibility to a disease, more animals can cross the threshold under the same environment. If the average susceptibility decreases, fewer animals cross. The change appears as a difference in prevalence.

Environment also changes the prevalence. Better sanitary management, less stress, adequate nutrition and more rigorous diagnosis can shift the distribution or change the practical threshold of observation. Therefore, the observed prevalence should not be automatically read as a genetic value. It is a phenotypic proportion recorded in a population, in an environment and with a classification criterion.

For pregnancy, reading is similar, but the central word is not susceptibility to the disease. The final record may be pregnant or empty, but the probability of pregnancy depends on a latent propensity involving female, male, management, health, nutrition and moment of evaluation. The threshold model helps not to treat "no" as a complete absence of biological merit. An empty mares may be close to reproductive success, but did not cross the point observed in that season.

Consider 10 genotypic mares for a didactic marker. The objective is not to associate this marker with a real characteristic; the goal is to train counting of genotypes and alleles.

| Genotype | Number of mares | Copies of `A` | Copies of `a` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `AA` | 3 | 6 | 0 |
| `Aa` | 4 | 4 | 4 |
| `aa` | 3 | 0 | 6 |
| Total | 10 | 10 | 10 |

First, it calculates genotypic frequencies. How `N = 10`, the frequency of `AA` is 3/10 = 0,30, the frequency of `Aa` is 4/10 = 0,40 and frequency of `aa` is 3/10 = 0,30. Biologically, this says that 30% of the mares observed are `AA`, 40% are heterozygous and 30% are `aa`.

Now calculate the frequency of the allele `A`:

`p = (2 x 3 + 4) / (2 x 10) = 10 / 20 = 0,50`

The value `p = 0,50` means that half of the allelic copies observed in this group are `A`. It does not mean that half of the mares are `AA`; this would be a confusion between allelic frequency and genotypic frequency.

Now calculate the frequency of the allele `a`:

`q = (2 x 3 + 4) / (2 x 10) = 10 / 20 = 0,50`

The value `q = 0,50` means that half of the allelic copies observed are `a`. As there are only two alleles in this example, `p + q = 0,50 + 0,50 = 1,00`.

See why heterozygotes count matters. If someone ignored `Aa`, they would only count 6 copies of `A` coming from `AA` and 6 copies from `a` comingfrom `aa`. This error would lose 8 Allelic copies loaded by heterozygous mares. In a small population, this type of error changes the interpretation of the most common allele.

Consider 100 candidate stallions evaluated by didactic performance index. The creator selects the 20 best, that is, 20% of the group.

| Group | Number of animals | Index average |
|---|---:|---:|
| All candidates | 100 | 100 |
| Selected | 20 | 120 |

The selection differential is:

`S = 120 - 100 = 20`

The selected ones are, on average, 20 points above the average of the candidates. This is the effect of the sieve. Now use the heritability of the characteristic:

`h2 = 0,30`

The expected answer is:

`R = h2 * S = 0,30 * 20 = 6`

Interpretation: If the assumptions of the didactic model are reasonable, the average of the next generation should increase about 6 points in the index. The expected average of offspring is not 120 points. It is:

`media_proxima_geracao = 100 + 6 = 106`

This point avoids a common error. The average of the selected parents does not automatically turn the average of their offspring. The expected response is filtered by the heritability, the quality of the evaluation and the model conditions.

Now consider generation interval:

| Item | Value |
|---|---:|
| `R` | 6 points per generation |
| `L` | 8 years |
| `ganho_por_ano` | 0,75 point per year |

If the generation interval was 6 years, keeping `R = 6`, the annual gain would be `6 / 6 = 1` point per year. Therefore, reducing generation interval can increase gain by time, even when the response per generation does not change. In horses, this decision needs to be biologically and operationally plausible; it is not enough to want short generation if the evaluation and reproduction system does not allow.

`media_parental = (210 + 220) / 2 = 215`

Consider eight horses in a didactic example of height. Each animal has three loci, and each locus can contribute to 0, 1 or 2 units. First we will ignore the environment to see only the polygenic sum.

| Animal | `L1` | `L2` | `L3` | `G = L1 + L2 + L3` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| B | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| C | 1 | 1 | 1 | 3 |
| D | 1 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
| E | 2 | 1 | 1 | 4 |
| F | 2 | 2 | 1 | 5 |
| G | 2 | 2 | 2 | 6 |
| H | 0 | 2 | 0 | 2 |

Animal A has low sum, `G = 1`. The animal G has high sum, `G = 6`. Among them are intermediate values: 2, 3, 4 and 5. This is the first important point. Even with only three loci, the characteristic no longer seems to be a simple division into two classes.

The average of `G` in this group is:

`media = (1 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 2) / 8 = 28 / 8 = 3,5`

The average value of the group is 3,5 units. Animals A and H are below average; D and E are slightly above; G is well above. The average helps to locate the center, but the table shows that there is variation. If we only looked at the average, we would lose the information that there are animals from 1 to 6 units.

Now add a didactic environmental deviation:

| Animal | `G` | `E` | `P = G + E` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| B | 3 | 0 | 3 |
| C | 3 | -1 | 2 |
| D | 4 | 1 | 5 |
| E | 4 | 0 | 4 |
| F | 5 | -1 | 4 |
| G | 6 | 0 | 6 |
| H | 2 | 1 | 3 |

The environment does not create polygenics, but changes the observed value. C and B have the same `G = 3`, but end up with different phenotypes because their environmental deviations are different. D and F have different genotypic values, but are close to the observed phenotype. This is the link with M6: the phenotype is still a sum of genotype and environment. The novelty of M7 is that the didactic genotype can be seen as a sum of many small effects.

Consider body weight and fat thickness in young horses. The values below are didactic. First, calculate a simple phenotypic correlation:

| Item | Value |
|---|---:|
| `covxy` | 6 |
| `vx` | 16 |
| `vy` | 9 |

The calculation is:

`r = covxy / sqrt(vx * vy)`

`r = 6 / sqrt(16 * 9)`

`r = 6 / sqrt(144)`

`r = 6 / 12 = 0,50`

Biologically, `r = 0,50` indicates moderate positive association. In the phenotypic example, heavier horses tend to have greater fat thickness. This does not yet say if the association is genetic, environmental or mixed.

Now compare three didactic correlations for the same characteristics:

| Correlation | Value | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| `rP` | 0,50 | Weight and fat phenotypes rise together in the observed lot |
| `rA` | 0,70 | Additive genetic values tend to move weight and fat together |
| `rE` | 0,20 | Environment also pushes the two characteristics in the same direction, but less |

In this scenario, selecting for higher weight tends to increase fat by genetic correlated response, because `rA` is positive and high. If the objective of the program is to increase weight without raising excessive fat, there is trade-off. The problem is not "weight is bad"; the problem is that improving one characteristic can move another in an unwanted direction.

Now imagine another scenario:

| Correlation | Value | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| `rP` | 0,50 | Phenotypes seem to be associated |
| `rA` | 0,05 | Additive genetic association is almost null |
| `rE` | 0,70 | Observed association comes mainly from the environment |

Here, looking only at `rP` could deceive. The heavier animals also seem fatter in the phenotype, but the additive genetic binding is weak. The genetic correlated response expected when selecting weight would be small. The environment, such as diet or management, explains much of the association observed.

Phenotypic correlation responds to what is observed. If `rP` between weight and fat is positive, heavier animals tend to be fatter in the evaluated group. This information is useful for lot description, but not enough to predict genetic consequence of selection.

Additive genetic correlation responds to what can change together by selection. If `rA` is positive between weight and fat, selecting for weight tends to increase fat by correlated response. If excessive fat is unwanted, the program needs to balance the two characteristics. If `rA` is negative, selecting weight could reduce fat. If `rA` is close to zero, weight selection tends to have little genetic consequence on fat.

The `rA` signal informs the direction of the correlated response. Positive value indicates a trend of change in the same direction; negative value indicates trend in opposite directions. The magnitude of `rA` indicates the strength of the genetic association: `rA = 0,70` suggests a stronger genetic bond than `rA = 0,05`. Still, the final size of the correlated response also depends on the selection applied in the main characteristic and on the variances and heritabilities involved. Therefore, the correlation guides the interpretation, but should not be read as an isolated guarantee.

Environmental correlation responds to what the environment moves together. More energy diet can increase weight and fat at the same time, generating `rE` positive. Management that improves physical conditioning can increase performance and reduce fat, generating negative environmental correlation in another example. Therefore `rE` helps explain the appearance of phenotypes, but should not be confused with genetic transmission.

Correlated response is the change in one characteristic when the selection was applied to another. If I select weight and `rA` fat is positive, fat tends to rise together. This is the trade-off. Improve a feature can worsen another when the objective of the program values different directions.

The `rA` signal informs the direction of the correlated response. Positive value indicates a trend of change in the same direction; negative value indicates trend in opposite directions. The magnitude of `rA` indicates the strength of the genetic association: `rA = 0,70` suggests a stronger genetic bond than `rA = 0,05`. Still, the final size of the correlated response also depends on the selection applied in the main trait and on the variances and heritabilities involved. Therefore, the correlation guides the interpretation, but should not be read as an isolated guarantee.

Environmental correlation responds to what the environment moves together. More energy diet can increase weight and fat at the same time, generating `rE` positive. Management that improves physical conditioning can increase performance and reduce fat, generating negative environmental correlation in another example. Therefore `rE` helps explain the appearance of phenotypes, but should not be confused with genetic transmission.

Correlated response is the change in one trait when the selection was applied to another. If I select weight and `rA` fat is positive, fat tends to rise together. This is the trade-off. Improve a feature can worsen another when the objective of the program values different directions.

Heterosis, or hybrid vigor, is the deviation of the mean cross-generation in relation to the parental mean. If the average of the offspring `F1` is higher than the mean of the two parental groups, the heterosis is positive for that characteristic. If it is equal, there is no average gain in relation to the parental average. If it is smaller, heterosis is negative for that characteristic.

Complementarity is different. It does not require `F1` to exceed the parental average. It requires that the groups have different and useful functions in the system. A didactic example: a maternal line can be chosen for fertility and easy management; a paternal line can also be chosen by performance in proof. Progeny can be recommended because it combines functions, even if not all features present positive heterosis.

Maternal breed is the genetic origin used on the female side. In many systems, this side weighs on fertility, childbirth, offspring, temperament and adaptation. Paternal breed is the genetic origin used on the male side. In many systems, this side weighs in performance, growth, conformation or terminal characteristic. These functions are not fixed laws; they are planning choices.

Fixed effect is a source of variation that we want to compare directly. Farm and sex are good didactic examples because the student can see the groups. If males are heavier on average, the effect of sex should be considered before comparing individuals. If a farm improves the weight of all animals, the effect of the farm also needs to be considered.

Random effect represents deviations from a larger population of possibilities. In simple language, we are not only interested in that specific level, but in the variability that this type of effect brings. In animal breeding, genetic effects of animals can be treated in this way in mixed models. The M16 only opens the conceptual door: `u` is the random part of the model.

Residue is the difference between the observed and predicted by the model. If a foal weighs more than the model expected after considering farm and sex, the residue will be positive. If it weighs less, it will be negative. Large residue may indicate unusual measurement, absent factor in the model or unexplained individual variation.

The error that M16 avoids is to compare animals as if they had all been measured in the same ruler. In real data, almost never are. Linear and mixed models are ways to declare the ruler used, adjust known effects and separate what was still unexplained.

In a real panel, there are thousands of SNPs. The student should not look at marker by marker without abstract. A histogram of MAF shows how many SNPs have little or much variation. In this class, the didactic version begins with a table:

| SNP | Frequency of the counted allele | Frequency of the other allele | MAF | Reading |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `SNP1` | 0,4 | 0,6 | 0,4 | more informative in the example |
| `SNP2` | 0,1 | 0,9 | 0,1 | low variation |
| `SNP3` | 0,9 | 0,1 | 0,1 | common allele, another rare allele |

The textual mini-histogram is:

| MAF | SNPs in the example |
|---|---|
| 0,0 a 0,2 | `SNP2`, `SNP3` |
| 0,2 a 0,4 | none |
| 0,4 a 0,5 | `SNP1` |

The history of the data is clear: `SNP1` separates the five horses better because there is more balance between alleles. `SNP2` and `SNP3` show little variation in the set, although for opposite reasons. Phenotype observed is the gross measure of the animal. It can be score in test, weight, height, fertility, progress, time, score or other record. Corrected phenotype is the phenotype adjusted to make the comparison fairer. In this unit, the correction will be explained in a simple way, without entering the linear models of M16.

`EBV` means estimated genetic value, in English `Estimated Breeding Value`. It estimates the additive genetic value of the animal for a trait. In practical terms, `EBV` answers: what is the estimated genetic merit of this animal as a breeder?

`DEP` means expected difference in progeny. In many didactic applications, `DEP` is half of `EBV`, because the father transmits a sample of half of his alleles to his offspring. Therefore, the simple formula of this unit is:

`DEP = EBV / 2`

Accuracy is a measure of confidence in prediction. High accuracy does not mean that the animal is good; it means that its estimate is more reliable. Low accuracy does not mean that the animal is bad; it means that there is more uncertainty. Accuracy also does not transform the `EBV` into definitive truth nor improves the animal's merit; it describes the risk of the estimate changing when new data enters. The ranking needs to consider estimated merit and information security.

Positive heterosis indicates that the cross overcame the parental mean for a trait. This can be useful in characteristics linked to vigor, fertility, survival or performance, but needs to be observed in the real system. Heterosis measured in one trait does not allow to conclude gain in all. One characteristic may have positive heterosis, another may be neutral, and another may worsen.

Complementarity appears when the crossing combines functions. If the maternal race contributes adaptation, fertility and temperament, and the paternal race contribute performance and conformation, the crossing can make sense even if some characteristics do not show high heterosis. The focus is the fit between objective and function of each group.

The didactic risk is to sell crossing as an automatic solution. Crossing different animals can bring heterosis, but it can also bring variability, loss of uniformity, management problems, incompatibility with racial record or poor result for non-measured characteristics. That's why crossing is a tool, not a shortcut.

It is also a mistake to confuse crossing with selection abandonment. Within each breed or lineage, it is still necessary to choose good breeders. A crossing between bad animals is not good because of the word "heterosis". The basis remains evaluation, objective and comparison.

Imagine that the animal has a biological recipe. DNA is the material where the recipe is written. A gene is a specific instruction within this recipe. An allele is a version of this instruction.

If the instruction was "type of characteristic visible in the coat", an animal could receive a version `A` of the father and a version`a` of his mother. The pair received forms the genotype at that point: `AA`, `Aa` or `aa`. What we observe in the animal, as presence or absence of the trait, is the phenotype.

The didactic care here is not to change the words:

- `A` or `a` are alleles.
- `AA`, `Aa` and `aa` are genotypes.
- The observed characteristic is phenotype.

This separation avoids a common error: looking at the animal and finding that it already knows exactly the pair of alleles he carries. The phenotype may help to raise a hypothesis, but it does not replace the reading of the genotype.

before:
Imagine three buttons that control the intensity of a lamp. Each button may be 0, 1 or 2. If only one button existed, there would be few possible intensities. With three buttons, more combinations appear. With ten or twenty buttons, the number of combinations is large. Even when each individual button has a small effect, the sum of the buttons can generate many final values.

With horses, we will use height at the heartwood as an example. A single didactic locus can contribute with 0, 1 or 2 units for the genotypic value. Three loci can produce sums from 0 to 6. Not all animals will have the same set of values. Some will have low sum, many will be around the medium and some will have high sum. When we add more loci and small environmental differences, the observed result seems to be a continuous range, not two or three rigid classes.

The error we want to avoid is to search for a single gene to explain alone a complex metric characteristic. There may be a gene of great effect in some cases, but the basic logic of quantitative genetics begins when many small effects add up. Griffiths et al. (2016) use the distinction between continuous and discontinuous variation as a central genetic problem. In this unit, we will train this difference with a small simulation, because it allows us to see the sum happening step by step.

Greater phenotype is not enough because phenotype genetic mixture and environment. An animal may seem superior because it is in better management, age, lot, training or opportunity. Corrected phenotype improves comparison, but it is still not the same thing as transmissible genetic merit.

`EBV` approximates the estimated additive genetic value. As selection seeks to change the next generation, `EBV` is central to breeder ranking. The animal with the highest `EBV` tends to have greater genetic merit estimated for the evaluated trait, provided that the evaluation has been done with adequate data.

`DEP` translates `EBV` into progeny expectation. When we say that a stallion has `DEP = 10`, we are talking about the expected average difference in offspring in relation to the base. This helps the creator to think about the effect of the breeder on the next generation, not only on his own performance.

Accuracy protects against naive decision. A young animal may have `EBV` high, but low accuracy because there are few own data, few relatives evaluated or little progeny information. A more proven animal may have a slightly lower `EBV`, but high accuracy. There is no automatic response; there is a risk criterion. The central point is to defend the ranking, not looking for a magic number.

Matrix `G` informs molecular similarity. It helps when the pedigree does not capture all the real variation shared between animals. However, `G` does not choose breeder alone. It answers who is more similar to the set of markers.

GWAS search for regions associated with a characteristic. It can generate biological cues, but should not be confused with immediate causal evidence. A peak can appear by connection with causal variant, population structure, family effect, residual error or statistical chance. Therefore, peak needs criticism and validation.

Genomic prediction has another objective: to estimate future merit, especially in young animals. GBLUP uses the `G` matrix within a prediction logic. The central question is not "what SNP has gained?", but "does the set of markers predict well new animals?". This question requires validation.

Prediction accuracy protects against false enthusiasm. A young animal with high prediction may seem excellent, but if the validation of the model is weak, the decision becomes risky. Eler (2017) treats accuracy as part of the reading of predictions; the same caution applies here. Prediction only has practical value when its performance was tested in a way compatible with the decision.

before:
BLUP avoids treating gross observation as if it were genetic value. A young animal may seem excellent in a test, but still have little evidence. The model pulls the estimate to a region more compatible with heritability, residue, fixed effects and family information. This movement protects against unstable ranking.

The animal model places each animal within the system as having an estimated additive genetic value. Instead of evaluating only proven breeders or only family means, the model allows the use of own records, relatives, pedigree and fixed effects in the same reasoning. The `A` matrix is the map that informs the model who is related to whom.

`lambda` regulates the force of penalization on random genetic effects. When `lambda` is high, individual information needs to be stronger to remove `EBV` from the average. When `lambda` is low, the model allows greater distance because the additive genetic variation has greater relative weight. Therefore change `h2` in the script changes the didactic `EBV`.

Accuracy is not praise to the animal. Accuracy is information about the stability of prediction. An animal can have `EBV` high and low accuracy; another may have `EBV` lower and high accuracy. The first can be promising, but uncertain. The second may be less extreme, but better known. Selection decision needs to declare whether it accepts more risk to seek greater expected gain or if it prefers more stable estimate.

The error that M17 avoids is to call genetic superiority what is only gross deviation. The second error avoided is to discard relatives as if each animal were an island. BLUP and animal model exist because both extremes are bad: believe only in the phenotype itself or ignore the kinship network.

before:
The general model of this unit is:

`y = Xb + Zu + e`

This formula seems abstract, but each part has a concrete function. `y` is the vector of observed phenotypes, such as weights in kg. `X` is a matrix that connects each observation to fixed effects. `b` is the vector of fixed effects, such as farm and sex. `Z` is a matrix that connects each observation to random effects. `u` is the vector of random effects. `e` is the residue, that is, the part that the model did not explain.

The student does not need to mount `X` and `Z` manually in this unit. The point is to understand that these matrices tell which line of data belongs to which effect. If the animal `A` is on the farm `Boa` and is male, the corresponding line in `X` marks these groups. If any effect is random, `Z` plays a similar role for the random part of the model.

In a simple reading, `Xb` represents known corrections or groups that we want to explicitly compare. Farm and sex can enter as fixed effects when the interest is to correct those specific groups. Already `Zu` represents effects that vary as deviations from a larger population. In animal breeding, genetic effects of animals can be treated in mixed models, but M16 does not estimate `EBV`, does not make BLUP and does not calculate animal model. This is for M17.

Residue is not statistical waste. Residue is information about what was left out of the model: measurement error, individual difference not explained, uncontrolled environmental variation or factors that were not recorded. If residues are very different between farms, this suggests that the model is not yet explaining the structure of the data.

before:
The main result of the unit is that a quantitative characteristic can gradually vary because many small effects add up. It is not necessary to have a simple biological category for each observed value. One horse slightly taller than another may not have "the gene of height"; it may have a slightly different combination of many loci and also have gone through a different environment.

The average summarizes the group, but does not replace the distribution. Two sets of horses can have similar average height and, even so, one group can be more uniform and another more spread. For genetic improvement, this distinction is essential because decisions made only based on the center of the group hide the variation between animals. In this unit, however, the conclusion must be at the initial level: quantitative genetics looks at measures, means and distribution, not only for simple Mendelian classes.

The simulation with three loci also shows a limitation. Three loci still produce few possible values. The distribution is closer to a continuous range when we increase the number of loci, the number and admit small environmental differences. Therefore, the example is a miniature. It does not intend to represent all the biology of height in horses; it serves to show why polygenic sums generate many intermediate values.

before:
The kg below are didactic genotypic values. They serve to train table reading and deviation calculation; they are not real foal measurement.

| Genotype | Genotypic value, kg |
|---|---:|
| `AA` | 10 |
| `Aa` | 8 |
| `aa` | 4 |

Step 1: calculate the mean point of homozygotes.

`M = (10 + 4) / 2 = 7`

The value 7 kg is what we would expect for `Aa` if the heterozygous was exactly in the middle between the two homozygosity.

Step 2: compare `Aa` with this mean point.

`D_Aa = 8 - 7 = 1`

The heterozygous was 1 kg above the midpoint. Biologically, in the example, the combination `Aa` did not behave as the perfect mean of `AA` and `aa`. It was closer to the high value.

Now see an interaction between two loci:

| Component | Expected value, kg |
|---|---:|
| contribution of locus A | 8 |
| contribution of locus B | 2 |
| expected sum | 10 |
| value of the combination `AaBb` | 13 |

`I_AB = 13 - (8 + 2) = 3`

The value 3 kg is the part of the combination that was not explained by the simple sum of the two loci. This is the didactic sign of positive epistasis: the combination between loci added value beyond the expected sum.

If the observed value of `AaBb` was 9 kg, the calculation would be:

`I_AB = 9 - (8 + 2) = -1`

In this case, epistasis would be negative in the example: the two loci together would deliver 1 kg below the expected sum.

before:
For two alleles, use:

`p + q = 1`

Here, `p` is the frequency of the `A` allele, and `q` is allele `a` frequency. These values vary from 0 to 1 and represent proportions of allelic copies, not proportions of animals.

The genotypic frequencies expected under Hardy-Weinberg are:

`f_AA = p^2`

`f_Aa = 2pq`

`f_aa = q^2`

The term `p^2` represents the expected chance of receiving `A` in both copies. The term `q^2` represents the expected chance of receiving `a` in both copies. The term `2pq` represents the heterozygous, because `Aa` can be formed as `A` from one origin and `a` from the other, or in the reverse order.

To transform expected frequency into expected count, multiply by `N`:

`E_AA = Np^2`

`E_Aa = N2pq`

`E_aa = Nq^2`

Here, `E` means expected number of animals in each genotype. This expected count serves to compare with the observed table.

With three alleles, `A1`, `A2` and `A3`, the frequencies can be called `p`,`q` and`r`, with:

`p + q + r = 1`

The expected frequencies of homozygotes are `p^2`, `q^2` and `r^2`. The expected frequencies of heterozygotes are `2pq`, `2pr` and `2qr`. Eler (2017) highlights an important consequence: with multiple alleles, the proportion of heterozygotes may exceed 50%, reaching 2/3 when three allele have equal frequencies.

before:
Think about combining different tools for the same task. A hammer does not replace a mouth key. A mouth key does not replace a plier. Together, different tools can solve a task better than a tool alone, but only if the task really needs this combination.

At the intersection, the logic is similar. A maternal breed can be valued by fertility, maternal ability, temperament and adaptation. A paternal race can be valued by growth, performance, conformation or sports fitness. Complementarity happens when each side enters with a planned function.

Heterosis is another point. Sometimes the cross generation `F1` exceeds the average of the parents in a trait, such as survival, fertility, initial vigor or performance in a given index. Falconer and Mackay (1996) treat heterosis as mean change observed in crosses. However, heterosis is not universal guarantee. It depends on the characteristics, the crossed groups, the environment and the comparison criteria.

before:
Think of two thermometers connected by different cables. A thermometer measures weight. Another measures fat thickness. If both rise together, it may be because they are connected by the same genetic cable, the same environmental cable or by a mixture of the two. Looking only at the observed numbers does not show which cable is pulling.

If better fed horses become heavier and fatter, there is a positive environmental bond. This link appears in the phenotype, but does not automatically mean that selecting heavier animals will genetically increase the fat of offspring. To think about genetic change, the most important cable is `rA`.

If `rA` is positive between weight and fat, selecting for greater weight also tends to increase fat by correlated response. If excessive fat is unwanted, a trade-off appears: improving weight can bring a bad consequence in another characteristic. If `rA` is negative, selecting weight can reduce fat. If `rA` is close to zero, the correlated genetic response tends to be small, even if there is phenotypic correlation caused by the environment.

With animals, the reasoning is similar. A stallion may have a high phenotype because it was created in a better environment, trained earlier, measured at favorable age or compared in a less demanding group. Another may have a lower phenotype, but in a more difficult condition. The corrected phenotype tries to make the comparison fairer.

After correction, we still need to separate what the animal shows from what he tends to transmit. `EBV` tries to estimate the additive genetic merit of the animal. `DEP` translates this merit to the average expectation in the offspring. Accuracy helps to say if the estimate is more firm or uncertain. Eler (2017) deals with genetic values, prediction and accuracy in the selection context; Falconer and Mackay (1996) reinforce that response to selection depends on genetic values and model assumptions.

Similarly, a small mean change in the underlying scale can produce a great change in prevalence when many animals are close to the cut-off point.

before:
When `h2` is low, the phenotypic difference between animals has little additive fraction in the example. For selection among breeders, this suggests that a single individual measure can be little informative about what will be transmitted to offspring. A better decision may require more evaluated animals, relatives, progeny or complementary information. The exact response depends on the evaluation design, but the logic is that low additive fraction reduces the confidence in the genetic prediction made from the simple phenotype.

When `h2` is high, the phenotypic variation is more connected to the additive part. This does not make selection automatic or perfect, but increases the usefulness of the phenotype to predict additive genetic differences. Even so, environment, scale and protocol remain important.

When repeatability is low, measuring again the same animal tends to be useful, because a single measure has a lot of temporary noise. When repeatability is high, a measure can better represent the individual pattern, and additional measures tend to add less information about the animal's own position. Therefore, the decision "measure more animals or measure more times" depends on the question.

Selection is the choice of animals that will be used as parents of the next generation. In this class, selection means choosing the 20% best stallions based on a didactic performance index. The index is in points and serves only to train the calculation.

The selection differential, `S`, is the difference between the average of the selected animals and the mean of the candidate population:

`S = media_dos_selecionados - media_da_populacao`

If the average of all candidates is 100 points and the average is 120 points, then `S = 20` points. Biologically, this means that the chosen parents are 20 points above the average of the candidates in the evaluated criterion.

The response to selection, `R`, is the expected change in the average of the next generation, in the same unit of the characteristic. In the simple model of the unit:

`R = h2 * S`

This response is expected, not guaranteed. It is used as a didactic approach for a generation and depends on the population, the characteristic, the environment, the quality of the evaluation and the adequacy of the model. Eler (2017) presents response to selection as a central theme of genetic prediction. Falconer and Mackay (1996) relate differential, selection intensity and expected response. Here we will use the shortest form because the unit needs to train basic reasoning before more complex models.

Selection intensity is the force of the sieve. Select 20% usually generates higher `S` than select 50%, if the animals were ordered by the same criterion. The intensity depends on the selected proportion and the distribution of the values. In this class, we calculate `S` directly by means, without using intensity tables.

Generation interval, `L`, is the average time between parents' generation and the generation of offspring used as new parents. If a generation takes 8 years, a response of 6 points per generation is equivalent to 0,75 point per year:

`ganho_por_ano = R / L = 6 / 8 = 0,75`

This annualized calculation is a way to see the effect of time. The main target of the class continues to be response per generation.

A gene is an inherited region associated with biological information. An allele is a variant of this gene. As horses are diploid organisms, in an autosomal simple locus each animal carries two copies: one inherited from the father and another inherited from his mother.

The genotype is the combination of these two copies. The phenotype is the observable characteristic. In a simple didactic characteristic, we can use:

| Genotype | Reading the allele pair | Didactic phenotype, by assumed rule |
|---|---|---|
| `AA` | two versions `A` | present characteristic |
| `Aa` | a `A` and a `a` version | characteristic present in the example |
| `aa` | two versions `a` | absent characteristic |

This table is a training model, not a general rule for horse coat. It serves to practice the difference between allele, genotype and phenotype without mixing several genes at the same time.

Critical point: in this example, observing the present characteristic does not separate `AA` from `Aa`. Both genotypes appear with the same didactic phenotype. The technical reason for this will be treated in the next unit; here, it is enough to recognize that observed phenotype and written genotype are not the same thing.

The value 0 represents absence of copies of the favorable allele in the example; the value 1 represents a copy; the amount 2 represents two copies. This coding is didactic. It does not affirm that every real gene acts like this, nor what horse height can be explained by only three loci. It serves to show the logic of the sum.

Continuous distribution, in the context of this unit, means that the observed values spread along a scale, with many possible values. In a small sample with few loci, the histogram will still have discrete bars. Even so, logic already appears: the more small loci enter the sum, the greater tends to be the number of possible combinations. When the environment also varies, close values can be further spread.

The average is the center of the group. One group can be very uniform; another can have very low and very high animals, even with a similar average.

Genotypic value is the number attributed to the expected effect of a genotype in the model. In this unit, we will use weight gain in kg as a didactic example. This number is not the observed weight of a specific foal; it is a value used to compare genotypes under a simplified condition.

Consider three genotypes in a locus:

| Genotype | Textual genotypic value, kg |
|---|---:|
| `AA` | 10 |
| `Aa` | 8 |
| `aa` | 4 |

If the action was strictly additive in this example, `Aa` would be at the average point of homozygotes:

`(10 + 4) / 2 = 7`

But the didactic value of `Aa` is 8. Therefore, the heterozygous is 1 kg above the midpoint. This deviation indicates partial dominance in the `AA` direction, because `Aa` was closer to `AA` than `aa`.

It is not enough to write "there is dominance". The direction matters. Dominance of `A` towards the high value is not the same thing as dominance of `a` towards low value.

before:
La analogía es el ADN como un mapa y una pista. A veces el mapa responde "¿quién está cerca de quién?". Esta es la cuestión de la matriz `G`. A veces el mapa muestra una región marcada con señal fuerte. Esta es la cuestión de GWAS. A veces utilizamos todo el mapa para estimar el camino probable de un animal joven antes de evaluar a muchos descendientes. Esta es la cuestión de la predicción genómica.

Matriz `G` es un mapa de parentesco molecular. Dos animales pueden tener pedigree similar, pero compartir más o menos marcadores de lo esperado. La matriz `G` trata de resumir esta similitud observada en los marcadores.

GWAS es una búsqueda local. Parece SNP para SNP y pregunta si algún marcador está asociado con la diferencia fenotípica. El resultado suele verse como trama de Manhattan: cada punto es un marcador, y los picos altos indican una asociación estadística más fuerte. Pico no es prueba automática del gen causal; es un punto que merece investigación.

La predicción genómica es el uso de todos los marcadores para predecir. En lugar de enfocarse en un pico, utiliza muchas señales pequeñas al mismo tiempo. GBLUP es una forma de predicción que utiliza el parentesco genómico, en matriz `G`, dentro de la lógica de los modelos mixtos. La pregunta práctica es: ¿La predicción funciona en animales que no fueron utilizados para entrenar el modelo?

before:
La analogía es ajustar una regla de torta antes de medir los animales. Si un gobernante comienza 2 cm por encima de cero, cada medida tomada con él es mayor. No vale la pena decir que un animal medido con este gobernante es más grande sin corregir el error del gobernante. Primero corrigimos el gobernante; luego comparamos los animales.

La granja puede funcionar como regla de torta. El sexo también puede funcionar así. Si los machos son más pesados en promedio que las hembras, compare a un macho de una buena granja con una hembra de una mala mezcla de animales granja, sexo y medio ambiente. El modelo trata de responder: ¿cuánto de la medida pertenece al grupo conocido y cuánto queda para el animal y para el error?

El efecto fijo es como una regla que queremos ajustar directamente. Si el curso compara exactamente dos granjas y dos sexos, podemos estimar la diferencia media entre estos grupos y corregir la medida. El efecto aleatorio es diferente: representa niveles considerados como una muestra de una mayor población de efectos. Residuo es lo que queda después de que el modelo explicara lo que se preveía en la fórmula.

before:
La analogía es limpiar el equilibrio antes de pesar un caballo. Si el equilibrio falla en un pesaje, la medida de ese animal es sospechosa. Si falla en muchos pesamientos, tal vez todo el equilibrio debe ser revisado. En datos genómicos, la lógica es similar: si un SNP falla en muchos animales, este marcador se vuelve sospechoso. Si un animal tiene muchos SNP desaparecidos, también se sospecha la muestra de ese animal.

La tasa de llamadas es la proporción de genotipos observados. Perder es la proporción de genotipos desaparecidos. Son complementarios. Si en cuatro animales uno SNP tiene tres genotipos observados y uno desaparecido, el desaparecido es `1/4 = 0,25` y la tasa de llamada es `3/4 = 0,75`.

MAF entra porque el marcador sin variación casi no ayuda a separar animales. Si casi todos los caballos tienen el mismo genotipo, que SNP lleva poca información en ese conjunto. HWE, o Hardy-Weinberg equilibrio, entra como un cheque de distribución genotípico. Una desviación muy fuerte puede indicar el error de genotipado, la estructura de la población, la selección, la insección u otro proceso. Por lo tanto, HWE debe ser utilizado como alerta, no como una frase automática.

La analogía es un comité antes de comprar o descartar a un criador. Un miembro mira el fenotipo. Otro cheque se dio lote, sexo, edad y gestión fueron tratados como fuentes de variación. Otro evalúa el pedigrí y el parentesco. Otro verifica si los datos genómicos se someten a control de calidad. Otra pregunta es si `EBV`, `DEP` y la precisión apoyan la elección.

Si cada miembro decide por sí solo, la conclusión puede ser mala. El fenotipo puede favorecer a los animales criados en un ambiente mejor. La genómica puede indicar un parentesco alto que aumenta el riesgo de apareamiento. El `DEP` puede ser bueno, pero con poca precisión. Pedigree puede ser interesante, pero los datos pueden ser incompletos.

El oleoducto completo organiza la conversación. Primero viene datos brutos. Entonces viene la limpieza. Luego viene corrección y predicción. Entonces viene la clasificación. Por último, hay un informe. El informe es la parte más importante del proyecto final: obliga al estudiante a defender la selección con pruebas, no preferiblemente.

before:
La analogía es un código de barra genética. Un código de barras de productos no describe todo el producto, pero ayuda a identificar patrones. A SNP El panel funciona de forma similar. No lee todo el genoma en detalle; observa muchos puntos específicos donde los animales pueden diferir.

A SNP es una variación en una posición de ADN. En una posición, algunos animales pueden tener el alelo `A` y otros pueden tener `B` el alele. Como los caballos son diploides, cada animal lleva dos copias de ese punto, una heredada del padre y una de la madre. Por lo tanto, si estamos contando el alelo `B`, el genotipo puede ser codificado como `0`, `1` o `2`.

El código `0` significa que no hay copia del alelo contado. El código `1` significa una copia. El código `2` significa dos copias. La biología detrás de ella es simple: `0` puede representar `AA`, `1` puede dar cuenta de `AB`, y `2` puede representar `BB`, cuando `B` es el alelo que estamos contando. La letra exacta depende del marcador; la lógica de contar es la misma.

before:
La analogía es una investigación con testigos familiares. La actuación del propio semental es un testigo directo. Dice algo importante, pero puede estar contaminado por medio ambiente, entrenamiento y oportunidad. El padre, la madre y los hermanos son testigos indirectos. No prueban todo sobre los jóvenes, pero ayudan cuando la prueba individual sigue siendo pequeña.

BLUP trabaja como evaluador que no cree ciegamente en ningún testigo. Si el animal tiene poco dado su propio, su estimación se dibuja a un promedio más seguro. Este movimiento se llama contracción. La rotura no castiga al animal. La rotura es reconocer que una diferencia observada aún no debe ser tratada como un mérito genético completo.

Los padres ayudan porque llevan información compartida. Un niño recibe, en promedio, la mitad del padre y la mitad de la información aditiva de su madre. Los semi-sibs comparten una fracción más pequeña. La matriz `A` organiza estas relaciones esperadas por el pedigree. Sin esta matriz, el modelo ve a los animales como independientes. Con esta matriz, el modelo sabe que el buen rendimiento de un relativo aumenta, con un peso limitado, la evidencia sobre los jóvenes.

before:
La fórmula central es:

`score = DEP - 10 * parentesco`

Donde:

- `DEP` se espera la diferencia en la progenie, en la unidad del índice de selección;
- `parentesco` es un riesgo medio o relativo relacionado con el grupo de mujeres planificado;
- `10` es una pena didáctica aplicada a los familiares;
- `score` es un valor utilizado para ordenar a los candidatos antes de la regla de calidad.

Si un semental tiene `DEP = 12` y `parentesco = 0,20`, entonces:

`score = 12 - 10 * 0,20 = 12 - 2 = 10`

Biológicamente, este animal todavía tiene una puntuación alta, pero pierde `2` puntos por riesgo de parentesco. La penalidad evita elegir automáticamente el más grande `DEP` cuando el apareamiento puede aumentar el encinamiento.

Si otro semental tiene `DEP = 9` y `parentesco = 0,02`, entonces:

`score = 9 - 10 * 0,02 = 8,8`

La primera sigue por encima, pero la diferencia cae. Este es el tipo de comparación que el proyecto final requiere: no es suficiente para mirar `DEP`; es necesario mirar la ganancia esperada junto con el riesgo.

before:
La fórmula de heredabilidad de la unidad es:

`h2 = VA / VP`

Donde:

- `h2` es la heredabilidad en el sentido restringido;
- `VA` es la varianza genética aditiva;
- `VP` es la diferencia fenotípica total.

La escala `h2` va de 0 a 1 en el ejercicio. Si `h2 = 0,10`, la fracción aditiva de variación fenotípica es baja. Si. `h2 = 0,60`, la fracción aditiva es alta. Estos valores son didácticos y dependen de la población, el medio ambiente, la característica y la forma de estimación.

Para la repetibilidad, utilizaremos una forma conceptual:

`r = variancia_permanente / VP`

Aquí, `variancia_permanente` representa diferencias que hacen que el mismo animal tiende a mantener una posición similar en medidas repetidas. Esta parte puede incluir efectos genéticos y entorno permanente. El entorno temporal, como una mala prueba en un día específico, está fuera de la parte permanente y reduce la similitud entre las medidas.

Interpretación corta:

- `h2` pregunta sobre los descendientes;
- `r` pregunta sobre la nueva medida del mismo animal;
- la precisión pregunta cuánta confianza da la información para decidir.

before:
La fórmula de correlación general es:

`r = covxy / sqrt(vx * vy)`

Donde:

- `r` es la correlación entre las características `x` y `y`;
- `covxy` es la covariancia entre `x` y `y`;
- `vx` es la diferencia de `x`;
- `vy` es la diferencia de `y`;
- `sqrt(vx * vy)` estandariza la covariancia para escala de -1 a 1.

Si `x` es peso y `y` es grosor de grasa, la fórmula mide cuánto el peso y las desviaciones de grasa van juntas, ajustando para el tamaño de la variación de cada característica.

Para diferentes tipos de correlación, la lógica es la misma, pero los componentes cambian:

`rP = covPxy / sqrt(VPx * VPy)`

`rA = covAxy / sqrt(VAx * VAy)`

`rE = covExy / sqrt(VEx * VEy)`

`rP` utiliza la covariancia y las diferencias fenotípicas. `rA` usa covarianza y variabilidades genéticas aditivas. `rE` utiliza covariance y varias ambientales. El error que queremos evitar es mirar `rP` y concluir automáticamente que la asociación es genética.

before:
La matriz `A` mantiene el parentesco aditivo esperado entre los animales. En un simple pedigrí, sin engendrar, la diagonal se puede leer como `1,00` para el animal con él mismo. De diagonal, padre e hijo han esperado parentesco `0,50`; madre e hijo `0,50`; semi hermanos paternos han esperado parientes `0,25`.

| Relación con `Jovem` | Paternidad aditiva prevista |
|---|---:|
| `Jovem` con él mismo | 1,00 |
| `Jovem` con el padre | 0,50 |
| `Jovem` con madre | 0,50 |
| `Jovem` with paternal half-sib | 0,25 |

Una representación didáctica de la matriz es:

| Animal | `Jovem` | `Pai` | `Mãe` | `Meio-irmão` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `Jovem` | 1,00 | 0,50 | 0,50 | 0,25 |
| `Pai` | 0,50 | 1,00 | 0,00 | 0,50 |
| `Mãe` | 0,50 | 0,00 | 1,00 | 0,00 |
| `Meio-irmão` | 0,25 | 0,50 | 0,00 | 1,00 |

El valor `0,00` entre padre y madre en el ejemplo no significa imposibilidad biológica general. Sólo significa que, en este pedigree didáctico, fueron tratados como no relacionados. Si hubiera parentesco o insección, la matriz cambiaría.

Ahora comparar crudo ranking y ranking por `EBV` didáctica:

| Animal | Desviación bruta | Pruebas familiares | `EBV` | Precisión cualitativa |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| `A_Jovem` | +20 | padre +12, madre +4 | 7,2 | moderada |
| `B_Provado` | +14 | descendientes evaluados | 10,0 | alto |
| `C_Jovem` | +18 | familia débil | 4,0 | bajo |

La columna de precisión es cualitativa. Se separa situaciones didácticas de baja, moderada y alta confianza, pero no calcula la exactitud real de cada animal.

El ranking bruto sería `A_Jovem`, `C_Jovem`,`B_Provado`. El ranking por didáctica `EBV` es `B_Provado`, `A_Jovem`,`C_Jovem`. Este cambio es la evidencia central de la unidad. El animal con la desviación bruta más alta no necesita ser el mejor criador estimado. Información familiar, cantidad de datos y lectura de cambios de precisión.

La selección es como un tamiz. Un gran tamiz pasa a muchos animales, incluyendo algunos sólo medianas. Un tamiz delgado deja pocos animales, generalmente el más alto en el criterio elegido. Cuanto más fino sea el tamiz, mayor es el promedio de los seleccionados en relación con el grupo promedio. Esta distancia es el diferencial de selección, `S`.

El tamiz Thiner aumenta la intensidad, pero también aumenta el riesgo. Si se utilizan pocos sementales, la elección se concentra más. Esto puede reducir las opciones de apareamiento, aumentar la dependencia de pocos animales y amplificar el error si la evaluación inicial está contaminada por medio del medio ambiente o la medición deficiente. La intensidad no es sinónimo de seguridad. Es una fuerza de selección aplicada a un criterio.

El intervalo de generación entra porque ganancia por generación y ganancia por tiempo no son lo mismo. Una respuesta de 6 puntos por generación parece buena, pero si cada generación toma 10 años, la ganancia anualizada es menor que en una especie o sistema con menor generación. En los caballos, el intervalo de generación suele ser una limitación práctica importante porque los sementales y las mares tienen un ciclo reproductivo más largo y un uso selectivo que en especies de producción de ciclo corto.

before:
BLUP significa `Best Linear Unbiased Prediction`, o mejor predicción lineal no sesgada. En la cría animal, BLUP se utiliza para predecir los efectos aleatorios, especialmente los valores genéticos aditivos. El término "mejor" depende de las suposiciones del modelo y de las diferencias utilizadas. Por lo tanto, BLUP no es una verdad biológica automática. Es una predicción estadística condicionada al modelo.

El modelo animal es un modelo mixto en el que cada animal recibe su propio efecto genético aditivo. La escritura básica es:

`y = Xb + Za + e`

En esta fórmula, `y` contiene los fenotipos observados; `Xb` representa efectos fijos, tales como granja, sexo o grupo contemporáneo; `Za` vincula cada observación al valor genético aditivo del animal; y `e` es el residuo. El vector `a` contiene los valores genéticos aditivos que se predicen. Cuando hablamos de `EBV`, estamos hablando de la estimación de estos valores genéticos aditivos.

La diferencia central en relación con M16 es que ahora el efecto aleatorio `a` no es una colección de desviaciones sueltas. Tiene covariancia dada por la matriz `A`. En forma conceptual:

`a ~ N(0, A * sigma_a^2)`

Esto significa que los valores genéticos aditivos de los animales están relacionados como se espera. Si dos animales están más relacionados, sus valores genéticos aditivos esperados tienen mayor covariancia. Si están menos relacionados, la covariancia esperada es menor. La matriz `A` es la forma numérica de colocar el pedigrí dentro del modelo.

Las ecuaciones modelo mixtas, o `MME`, reúnen efectos fijos y efectos aleatorios en un solo sistema. Para la lectura conceptual, una forma simplificada es:

`[X'X  X'Z; Z'X  Z'Z + A^-1 * lambda] [b_hat; a_hat] = [X'y; Z'y]`

El estudiante no necesita resolver esta matriz a mano en esta unidad. La fórmula sirve para localizar las piezas del modelo, no para entrenar álgebra de matriz. `X` ajusta los efectos fijos. `Z` une las observaciones a los animales. `A^-1` inserta el parentesco. `lambda` controla el peso relativo entre residuos y variación genética aditiva. Cuando el residuo pesa demasiado en relación con la genética aditiva, el modelo se contrae más `EBV` al promedio.

before:
La característica del Umbral es una característica observada en las categorías, pero interpretada como resultado de una escala subyacente continua. La categoría aparece cuando esta escala supera un umbral. En lugar de medir directamente la escala subyacente, observamos el resultado final: afectados o no afectados, embarazadas o vacías, vivos o muertos.

La sostenibilidad es la tendencia latente de un animal a expresar un resultado no deseado, como la enfermedad. Una mayor susceptibilidad significa una mayor posibilidad de cruzar el umbral de manifestación. Para los resultados deseados, como el embarazo o la supervivencia, se puede explicar la misma lógica como propensión latente al éxito. Esta distinción evita tratar cada resultado como si fuera enfermedad.

La prevalencia es la proporción de animales que aparece en la categoría de interés. Si 18 de 100 los caballos tienen una enfermedad, la prevalencia observada de la enfermedad es 18%. Si 72 de 100 mares están embarazadas, la prevalencia del embarazo es 72%. La prevalencia es observable; la escala subyacente es una manera didáctica de explicar por qué el registro sí / todavía no puede tener una base cuantitativa.

Griffiths et al. (2016) presentan ejemplos de características de susceptibilidad a las enfermedades y rasgos subyacentes estudiados por QTL. En esta clase, esta referencia se utiliza conservadoramente: apoya la idea de que los resultados categóricos o clínicos pueden estar vinculados a la variación genética y a los rasgos subyacentes. El modelo de umbral didáctico se utilizará aquí sólo para capacitar la interpretación de la escala subyacente, el umbral y la prevalencia.

before:
Las características del Umbral requieren precaución porque la categoría observada oculta distancia al umbral. Dos caballos no afectados pueden tener posiciones subyacentes muy diferentes. Dos lotes con la misma prevalencia pueden tener diferentes distribuciones subyacentes. Un montón puede tener muchos animales cerca del umbral y otro puede tener pocos.

La genética puede cambiar la respuesta sí/no contribuyendo al desplazamiento de la escala subyacente. Si un grupo tiene una mayor susceptibilidad media a una enfermedad, más animales pueden cruzar el umbral bajo el mismo ambiente. Si la susceptibilidad promedio disminuye, menos animales se cruzan. El cambio aparece como una diferencia en la prevalencia.

El medio ambiente también cambia la prevalencia. Una mejor gestión sanitaria, menos estrés, una nutrición adecuada y un diagnóstico más riguroso pueden cambiar la distribución o cambiar el umbral práctico de la observación. Por lo tanto, la prevalencia observada no debe leerse automáticamente como valor genético. Es una proporción fenotípica registrada en una población, en un ambiente y con un criterio de clasificación.

Para el embarazo, la lectura es similar, pero la palabra central no es susceptibilidad a la enfermedad. El registro final puede estar embarazada o vacía, pero la probabilidad de embarazo depende de una propensión latente que involucre a mujeres, hombres, administración, salud, nutrición y momento de evaluación. El modelo de umbral ayuda a no tratar el "no" como una ausencia completa de mérito biológico. Las mares vacías pueden estar cerca del éxito reproductivo, pero no cruzaron el punto observado en esa temporada.

Es una proporción fenotípica registrada en una población, en un ambiente y con un criterio de clasificación.

Para el gestación, la lectura es similar, pero la palabra central no es susceptibilidad a la enfermedad. El registro final puede estar gestante o vacía, pero la probabilidad de gestación depende de una propensión latente que involucre a hembras, machos, administración, salud, nutrición y momento de evaluación. El modelo de umbral ayuda a no tratar el "no" como una ausencia completa de mérito biológico. Las yeguas vacías pueden estar cerca del éxito reproductivo, pero no cruzaron el punto observado en esa temporada.

before:
Considere 10 mares genotípicos para un marcador didáctico. El objetivo no es asociar este marcador con una característica real; el objetivo es entrenar el recuento de genotipos y alelos.

| Genotipo | Número de mares | Copia de `A` | Copia de `a` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `AA` | 3 | 6 | 0 |
| `Aa` | 4 | 4 | 4 |
| `aa` | 3 | 0 | 6 |
| Total | 10 | 10 | 10 |

Primero, calcula frecuencias genotípicas. ¿Cómo? `N = 10`, la frecuencia de `AA` es 3/10 = 0,30, la frecuencia de `Aa` es 4/10 = 0,40 y frecuencia de `aa` es 3/10 = 0,30. Biológicamente, esto dice que 30% de las mares observadas son `AA`, 40% son heterocigous y 30% son `aa`.

Ahora calcula la frecuencia del alelo `A`:

`p = (2 x 3 + 4) / (2 x 10) = 10 / 20 = 0,50`

El valor `p = 0,50` significa que la mitad de las copias alelicas observadas en este grupo son `A`. No significa que la mitad de las mares sean `AA`; esto sería una confusión entre la frecuencia alelica y la frecuencia genotípica.

Ahora calcula la frecuencia del alelo `a`:

`q = (2 x 3 + 4) / (2 x 10) = 10 / 20 = 0,50`

El valor `q = 0,50` significa que la mitad de las copias alelicas observadas son `a`. Como sólo hay dos alelos en este ejemplo, `p + q = 0,50 + 0,50 = 1,00`.

Vea por qué los heterocigotas cuentan cosas. Si alguien ignoraba `Aa`, sólo contarían 6 copias de `A` viniendo de `AA` y 6 copias de `a` viniendo de `aa`. Este error perdería 8 copias alelicas cargadas por mares heterocigous. En una pequeña población, este tipo de error cambia la interpretación del alelo más común.

| Animal | Granja | Sexo | Peso observado | Efecto agrícola | Efecto sexual | Peso ajustado |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `A` | Bien. | Hombre | 310 | +18 | +8 | 284 |
| `B` | Bien. | Mujer | 294 | +18 | 0 | 276 |
| `C` | Dry | Hombre | 292 | -10 | +8 | 294 |
| `D` | Dry | Mujer | 278 | -10 | 0 | 288 |

| semental | Fenotipo observado | Efecto ambiental | Fenotipo corregido |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `A` | 112 | +8 | 104 |
| `B` | 106 | -2 | 108 |
| `C` | 100 | 0 | 100 |

Si el ranking fuera hecho sólo por el fenotipo observado, el orden sería `A`, `B`,`C`. Después de la simple corrección, la orden cambia a `B`, `A`,`C`. El semental `A` parecía mejor, pero parte de la ventaja provenía del medio ambiente. El semental `B` tenía un fenotipo inferior, pero fue evaluado en una condición menos favorable.

Ahora compare `EBV`, `DEP` y la precisión:

| semental | `EBV` | `DEP = EBV / 2` | Precisión | Lectura |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `A` | 20 | 10 | 0,55 | mayor valor estimado, confianza moderada |
| `B` | 8 | 4 | 0,85 | fondo menor, estimación más firme |
| `C` | -4 | -2 | 0,70 | expectativa por debajo de la base |

El cálculo manual de `DEP` es:

`DEP_A = 20 / 2 = 10`

`DEP_B = 8 / 2 = 4`

`DEP_C = -4 / 2 = -2`

Biológicamente, `A` tiene mayor potencial promedio esperado para la progenie en este índice, pero su precisión es menor que la de `B`. Si el objetivo es maximizar la ganancia y aceptar más incertidumbre, `A` puede ser elegido. Si el objetivo es una decisión más conservadora, `B` puede ser defendido porque tiene menor `DEP`, pero mayor precisión. La elección debe declarar el criterio.

Considere un pedigree didáctico con caballos. El semental `S` tiene dos crías: `P` y `Q`. La madre de `P` es `M1`; la madre de`Q` es`M2`. Las madres no están relacionadas entre sí y no están estrechamente relacionadas con `S`. Ningún animal de la base está enredado.

| Animal | Padre | Madre | Observación |
|---|---|---|---|
| `S` | desconocida | desconocida | Base animal |
| `M1` | desconocida | desconocida | Base animal |
| `M2` | desconocida | desconocida | Base animal |
| `P` | `S` | `M1` | hijo de `S` |
| `Q` | `S` | `M2` | hijo de `S` |

`P` y `Q` son semi-sibs paternos. Comparten el semental. `S`Pero tienen madres diferentes. El parentesco aditivo esperado entre medio hermanos es:

`A_PQ = 0,25`

La matriz simplificada `A` para comparar sólo `P` y `Q` es:

| Animal | `P` | `Q` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `P` | 1,00 | 0,25 |
| `Q` | 0,25 | 1,00 |

Las diagonales son `1,00` porque `P` y `Q` no son enredados en este ejemplo. Las posiciones fuera de la diagonal son `0,25` porque son medio hermanos. La matriz es simétrica: la relación `P` con `Q` es igual a la relación con `Q` `P`.

Ahora imagina un apareamiento entre `P` y `Q`. Como son medio hermanos, la inspiración esperada de la descendencia `X` es:

`F_X = A_PQ / 2`

`F_X = 0,25 / 2 = 0,125`

`F_X = 12,5%`

En la matriz `A`, la diagonal del becerro sería:

`A_XX = 1 + F_X`

`A_XX = 1 + 0,125 = 1,125`

Este es el punto central de la clase. Parenting among parents appears as inbreeding in the offspring. La diagonal `1 + F` muestra que el becerro no es sólo "un animal más"; lleva información sobre la identidad por descendencia.

before:
El control de calidad protege el análisis de falsas conclusiones. A SNP con mucha falta puede parecer diferente entre los animales sólo por falta de lectura. A SNP con muy bajo MAF casi no separa individuos en ese conjunto. Una fuerte desviación de HWE puede indicar problemas técnicos, pero también puede reflejar la estructura de la población, el parentesco, el encinamiento o la selección. Por lo tanto, el filtro debe ser explicado, no aplicado como ritual.

La tasa de llamada por SNP responde: ¿Este marcador fue leído en animales suficientes? Tasa de llamada por animal responde: ¿tiene esta muestra suficientes genotipos para ser confiable? MAF respuestas: ¿Este marcador varía lo suficiente para informar cualquier diferencia? HWE respuestas: ¿La distribución de genotipos parece compatible con simple expectativa o merece revisión?

El error que M19 evita es el uso de matriz genómica sucia como si se le diera el final. En la cría de animales, el problema no es sólo estadística. Si un animal es quitado por baja calidad de genotipado, pierde información en el siguiente paso. Si un mal SNP permanece en la matriz, puede crear ruido. La decisión debe equilibrar la limpieza y la preservación de la información.

Lourenco et al. (2020) describen controles de calidad que incluyen SNPs de baja tasa de llamadas, Hardy-Weinberg desviaciones y tasas de llamadas bajas. En esta clase, convertimos esta idea en una escala manual para que el estudiante comprenda la razón de cada filtro antes de utilizar herramientas automáticas. Falconer y Mackay (1996) dan a la población base para pensar las frecuencias alelicas; aquí, esta base aparece en el relato de `p`, `q`,`MAF` y HWE.
